newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says signed budget only "to avoid turmoil".
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says signed budget only "to avoid turmoil".

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, harshly criticising his government and the communist-led opposition, said on Friday that Russia's 1997 budget was badly flawed and that he had signed it this week only to avoid political turmoil.
"A bad budget is no excuse to give up," he said.

In a brief radio address, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader made clear he was launching an energetic comeback after illness by saying that the only solution was for him to take a much bigger personal role in drafting next year's budget.

He avoided personal criticism of his prime minister, however, saying only: "Viktor Stepanovich Chernomyrdin has reported that even within the framework of the budget that was passed, it is possible to meet promises to pay people."

Russian media have speculated the 58-year-old premier, an icon of stability for the business community, could be sacked after Yeltsin's annual state of the nation address next Thursday partly because millions of workers and pensions are owed back pay.

"There are very major doubts that the budget is capable of being fulfilled," said Yeltsin, who has been out of action with heart trouble and then pneumonia for eight months -- his entire second term so far.

"I will tell you straight away that such a decision (signing the budget) did not come easily to me. There are major doubts about many key items," Yeltsin said, faulting the government for not working hard enough on the document.

He said its budget bill contained a host of "unrealistic articles" and that the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament had engaged in populism, damaging it further with its amendments.

"I signed it with a heavy heart. Because to send back the budget today would have meant pushing the political situation in the country to the limits of bitterness," Yeltsin said. "And a new wave of instability would hurt our most defenceless citizens hardest of all."
It would also have delayed the revival of the economy and made it harder to keep prices under control, he said.
The International Monetary Fund, which last year agreed to bankroll Russia to the tune of $10 billion over three years, is watching the government's budget performance closely.
